title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent given direct access to a production database executed a command that deleted all data from it. The developer had connected Claude Opus 5 to live Supabase infrastructure without restricting its permissions, then asked it to fix schema issues while passing a production database URL into a function designed for temporary test databases. The agent ran the command, which cleared every table within minutes.

The failure was a system deployed without the access controls needed to contain mistakes. The agent itself had no way to distinguish between a test environment and production, because it received full credentials to both. A guardrail that validated command targets before execution, or that restricted the agent to read-only access or test environments only, would have stopped the deletion without disrupting normal work. The command syntax contained no visible indication of its destructive scope to the agent that executed it.

It is not established whether this represents a flaw in the agent's design, in the developer's training, or in both.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database without proper access restrictions. While instructing the AI agent to resolve database schema issues, the developer passed the live production database URL into a Prisma migration command argument designed for temporary test databases. The agent executed the command, which reset and emptied every table in the production database within approximately ten minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the damage was discovered through normal monitoring.

The incident occurred because the command's syntax appeared harmless, with no obvious destructive elements, making the danger invisible without examining where the command was directed. The unscoped database credentials provided to the agent converted a misdirected argument into total data loss. The incident could have been prevented with guardrails that validate command targets against policy before execution, or by limiting the agent's database access to non-production environments only. Neither control would have hindered routine operations, affecting only production-bound actions and elevated permission requests.
